RQ1.question: Does knowing a ZIP's affordable-housing completions improve an out-of-time forecast of its injury crashes?
RQ1.sentence: The change in out-of-time forecast error from adding affordable-housing completions and stock is +0.60 injury crashes per ZIP per year (95% interval +0.17 to +1.10, n = 171 ZIP codes). The interval lies above zero, which fits a less accurate forecast.
RQ1.label: Forecast error when housing is added
RQ1.unit: MAE difference (injury crashes per ZIP per year)
RQ1.direction: right of zero = forecast less accurate with housing

RQ2.question: Within a ZIP over time, do injury crashes move as the cumulative stock of completed affordable units grows?
RQ2.sentence: The within-ZIP change in injury crashes as the stock of completed affordable units grows is +0.07 percent per 100 units (95% interval -0.06 to +0.41, n = 171 ZIP codes). The interval includes zero.
RQ2.label: Injury crashes as the unit stock grows
RQ2.unit: % change in injury crashes per 100 units
RQ2.direction: right of zero = more injury crashes with a larger stock

RQ3.question: Do injury crashes within 250 m of new-construction sites change after completion, relative to not-yet-completed sites?
RQ3.sentence: The after-against-before change in injury crashes within 250 m of new buildings, relative to comparison sites, is -4.6 percent (95% interval -11.9 to +3.3, n = 128 new-construction sites). The interval includes zero.
RQ3.label: After against before, new buildings
RQ3.direction: right of zero = more injury crashes after completion

RQ4.question: Does the before/after change in injury crashes at a new-construction site scale with the number of units?
RQ4.sentence: The slope of the after-against-before change in injury crashes on the units completed in that year within 250 m is -2.2 percent per doubling of units (95% interval -5.8 to +1.1, n = 128 new-construction sites). The interval includes zero.
RQ4.label: Change by units completed nearby
RQ4.direction: right of zero = larger rise where more units were completed

RQ5.question: Is the before/after change in injury crashes different near New Construction than near Preservation (the placebo)?
RQ5.sentence: The after-to-before ratio of injury crashes around new construction, relative to the same ratio around preservation, is -8.1 percent (95% interval -19.6 to +4.9, n = 306 completed sites). The interval includes zero.
RQ5.label: New construction against preservation
RQ5.unit: % difference between the two after/before ratios
RQ5.direction: right of zero = change more positive at new construction

RQ6.question: Does the pedestrian and cyclist share of injury crashes near sites change after completion?
RQ6.sentence: The gap in the pedestrian and cyclist share of injury crashes (completed minus comparison sites) is +1.22 percentage points (95% interval -1.08 to +3.39, n = 306 completed sites, against 696 comparison sites, in 409 clusters). The interval includes zero.
RQ6.label: Pedestrian and cyclist share
RQ6.unit: percentage points, completed minus comparison sites
RQ6.direction: right of zero = share rose more at completed sites

RQ7.question: Before the project starts, are new-construction sites on streets with more injury crashes than typical street locations of the borough?
RQ7.sentence: The mean borough percentile of new-construction sites, before their project started, minus 50 is +19.90 percentile points (95% interval +16.56 to +22.99, n = 2,789 new-construction sites in 336 one-kilometre blocks). The interval lies above zero, which fits sites standing where there were already more injury crashes than at the typical street point of the borough.
RQ7.label: Where new-construction sites stand before the project
RQ7.unit: percentile points above the typical street point of the borough
RQ7.direction: right of zero = more injury crashes than the typical street point

RQ8.question: Does the hour-of-day mix of injury crashes near sites shift after completion?
RQ8.sentence: The largest gap among the 4 parts of the day, the one for the share of injury crashes in the afternoon (12:00 to 17:59), with its interval widened for 4 tests, is +1.41 percentage points (99% interval -2.05 to +4.23, n = 306 completed sites, against 696 comparison sites, in 409 clusters). The interval includes zero.
RQ8.label: Hour of day (largest band gap)
RQ8.unit: percentage points; largest of 4 gaps, interval widened for 4 tests
RQ8.direction: right of zero = share rose more at completed sites

RQ9.question: Across ZIP codes, is the deep-affordable share associated with the pedestrian and cyclist share of harm?
RQ9.sentence: The within-borough rank correlation between the deep-affordable share and the pedestrian and cyclist share of injury crashes is -0.215 (95% interval -0.392 to -0.000, n = 123 ZIP codes in 5 boroughs). The interval excludes zero by 0.000, the p-value is 0.052 and 0.104 after adjustment for the two outcomes, so this is not counted as a difference from zero.
RQ9.label: Deep-affordable share and who is hurt
RQ9.direction: right of zero = higher pedestrian and cyclist share where the stock is deeper

RQ10.question: Which contributing-factor groups are over- or under-represented near completed housing, after against before?
RQ10.sentence: The largest gap among the 9 factor groups, the one for the share of "Impairment or medical" among injury crashes with a recorded factor, with its interval widened for 9 tests, is -0.83 percentage points (99% interval -2.76 to +0.67, n = 306 completed sites, against 696 comparison sites, in 409 clusters). The interval includes zero.
RQ10.label: Contributing factor (largest group gap)
RQ10.unit: percentage points; largest of 9 gaps, interval widened for 9 tests
RQ10.direction: right of zero = share rose more at completed sites
